Upto this point we have implemented quite a bit of building blocks. In implementing the ability to make function calls we bring lot of those blocks together. This was a long chapter and has a lot of content. To do justice to the topic I highly recommend reading the book. In this write up I am going to focus not so much on the implementation but on the salient ideas that stand out to me during the implementation.

Syntax for a function is `add(2, 3)`. The starting keyword - the callee / the function being called - in our Lox programming language `add` is an expression that gets evaluated. As such it could be an expression that evaluates to a function and is not part of the function call syntax. The elements within the parenthesis are arguments each of which are also expressions. 

Function Currying refers to returning returning partial function which itself take additional parameters. It is easier to illustrate with an example. `fn(1)(2)(3);` here `fn` is a function that takes one argument and returns another function that takes one argument which also returns a function that takes one argument which finally completes the chain of calls and execution ends. This style of chaining series of function calls is `Currying`. Programming langauge `Haskell` has this concept baked into the language. We have that support in Lox. 


```
def _call(self) -> Expr:
		"""Parse a function call."""
		expr: Expr = self._primary()

		while True:
				if self._match(TokenType.LEFT_PAREN):
						expr = self._finish_call(expr)
				else:
						break
		return expr

def _finish_call(self, callee: Expr) -> Expr:
		arguments: List[Expr] = []
		if not self._check(TokenType.RIGHT_PAREN):
				arguments.append(self._expression())
				while self._match(TokenType.COMMA):
						if len(arguments) >= MAX_ARGUMENTS:
								ErrorReporter.error_at_token(
										self._peek(),
										f"Can't have more than {MAX_ARGUMENTS} arguments.",
								)
						arguments.append(self._expression())
		paren: Token = self._consume(
				TokenType.RIGHT_PAREN, "Expect ')' after arguments."
		)
		return Call(callee=callee, paren=paren, arguments=arguments)
```

In the preceeding lines of code we have the logic of how `Currying` is implemented. `Call` is the AST node for the function call.

Capping the maximum number of arguments to be allowed in a funciton call. I never thought about this when using a language. In the Lox language we are restricting it to 255 arguments. Above that and we report an error; we do not terminate the program however. So, nothing stops a user from passing more arguments but the warning will be displayed.

What to do when a function is called with too many arguments? Looks like differnt languages handle this differently. JavaScript allows it and discards the excess parameters and fills in `undefined` value for missing arguments. Since Lox is a dynamic typed language we don't have static type checking so we follow python (dynamic language) and raise an `Error` when there is a mismatch in the number of parameters expected and received in a function call. Technical term for this is the "arity" of a function - expected number of arguments.

Native functions are functions that have operations implemented in the underlying language - in our case Python. These are part of the language and are made availabe to the user as convenient way to do useful things. For our case we implement a `clock` function which return number of seconds elapsed since a specific time. Native functions allow the user to do simple things without jumping through hoops for things like reading files etc.

Local function and Closure.

Lox supports local functions. Local functions are functions declared and used inside another function. Below is an illustration from the book: 

```
fun makeCounter() {
  var i = 0;
  fun count() {
    i = i + 1;
    print i;
  }

  return count;
}

var counter = makeCounter();
counter(); // "1".
counter(); // "2".
```
Here `makeCounter` returns a reference to the `count` local function. In order for this above example to work correctly the state of the local variable `i` needs to be preserved and updated. This idea of a reference function that wraps local variable reference is called `Closure` as an function closes over the variables. 

We accomplish this by creating an `Environment` - `self.closure` in below snippet - that captures the state of the function when it is declared. And when the function is called we refer to this environment instead of the global environment. 

```
class LoxFunction(LoxCallable):
    def __init__(self, declaration: Function, closure: Environment) -> None:
        self.declaration: Function = declaration
        self.closure: Environment = closure

    def call(self, interpreter: Interpreter, arguments: List[object]) -> object:
        environment: Environment = Environment(enclosing=self.closure)
        for parameter, argument in zip(self.declaration.params, arguments):
            environment.define(parameter.lexeme, argument)

        try:
            interpreter.execute_block(self.declaration.body, environment)
        except Return as return_signal:
            return return_signal.value
        return None
```

That is all I have to say about that.
